newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Armed guards may be sent to protect D.C. schools.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Armed guards may be sent to protect D.C. schools.

text.p: The retired Army general who was handed control of the U.S. capital's collapsing public school system says he may send guards armed with guns into the city's worst schools to end the violence.

Julius Becton Jr. also says he is close to approving a security plan that will make it harder for students to smuggle weapons into schools. Like civilians stranded in a war zone, some teachers and students at McKinley High at Second and T streets in Northeast Washington are angry about the plan, about the need for it, about everything.

"These kids are not criminals, they are students," a guidance counsellor said as she surveyed a group of teenagers smoking cigarettes, laughing and jostling during a break near the squalid, block-long brick school within shouting distance of the U.S. Capitol. "Half of them will go on to college," she said in defence of her students.

"Would you want armed men in your child's school? What has it come to?" She shrugs, asking that her name not be printed for fear that the general might retaliate for her opposition to the armed guard plan.

McKinley, where two girls were stabbed on the same day this month and a local radio reporter was beaten when he went to the scene, is one of the schools where security is to be tightened. Becton, named as the Washington school system's new chief executive officer by a financial control board that has taken over running the near-bankrupt city, says security is a top priority. His motto is: "Failure is not an option."

The board turned to Becton, who once ran the Federal Emergency Management Agency, after a scathing report gave the elected school board and Superintendent Franklin Smith an "F" grade for failing to stop the school system's dowward spiral.

The control board said the elected board spent more time in meetings discussing parking privileges and their salaries than school problems. Meanwhile, crime is soaring in the city's schools, up 60 percent from a year ago. At least twice a day police cars race to a city school to arrest students or hangers-on for crimes ranging from murder to beatings, sexual assaults, theft, robberies and bomb threats. Teachers have been accused 35 times this year of hitting students.

A firm from McLean, Virginia, has been hired to provide the city's 158 schools with 223 guards. They have given Becton a plan to used armed police officers, security guards, cameras and metal detectors to stop students smuggling in weapons.

Security may be a top priority for Becton but there is a long list of shortcomings he must deal with from dilapidated buildings to shortages of equipment, from leaking gyms to test scores ranking Washington students at or near the bottom. Spending more money per pupil than any other U.S. city -- more than $8,000 a year -- and providing a lower student-to-teacher ratio than even the wealthiest suburbs has not helped.

For the past 20 years, student achievement as judged by virtually every standard has fallen short of the national average by a wide mark, scoring at or near the bottom in every comparison of the 50 states and the District of Columbia. The dropout rate of students quitting high school is about 40 percent, near the highest for any city in the United States. On any given day, one out of 10 who remain enrolled simply do not show up, according to school officials.

Student enrollment has fallen to just under 79,000 from a peak in 1970 of nearly 150,000 and some schools operate at just 60 percent of capacity. White flight to the suburbs in the 1960s and 1970s, followed by a surge of middle class blacks who moved mainly to nearby Maryland, sped the decline.
The students who remain are poorer. Students receiving welfare account for nearly half the population, up from 26 percent just in the past five years.

Abdusalam Omer, imposed as chief financial administrator for the schools, told the financial control board the system was on the verge of collapse because of long-term neglect and mismanagement. He said the administration had spent $54 million more than its budget over the past five years and could not properly account for hundreds of employees.

Colbert King, a member of the Washington Post editorial board, said, "The kindest thing to be said of the D.C. school system's approach to management and administration is that it's ... all huffing and puffing, frowning and fussing, kee-keeing and caw-cawing, picking up paychecks while moaning the 'Mo Money Blues.'"

Mayor Marion Barry was on an "image-building" trip to Asia this month when the control board took over the school system. Announcing at a news conference that he had lured a Chinese firm to open a Peking duck restaurant in the U.S. capital, Barry said he was helpless to stop the school takeover.
"We know that the school board has flunked. They (the control board) were determined to do what they had to do."
